To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have performed a quantum state-resolved study of the vibrational excitation of the dissociative adsorption of methane on Pt(111) and that we have observed a significant effect of symmetry on the dissociation probability.

we have measured state-resolved reactivities of the 2 ν3 antisymmetric stretch of CH4 on the Pt(111) and Pt(110) surfaces and that we have shown that the E symmetry component of the 2nu3 antisymmetric stretch vibration of methane is less reactive than the A1 and E2 symmetry components.
the symmetry of the vibrational excitation state plays a role in the vibrational activation process of methane chemisorption.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the fundamental understanding of the role of symmetry on the vibratonal activation of chemical reactions.
the fundamental aspects of the interaction of gas phase molecules with surfaces.
the role of vibratinal symmetries on the vibrational excitation of the dissociative adsorption of CH4 on a Pt(111) substrate.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the symmetry of the vibrational excitation plays a minor role in the vibrational activation process of the dissociative adsorption of methane on Pt(111).
the vibrational symmetry of the C-H stretching vibrations of methane plays a role in its reactivity on Pt(111), but that the effect is not as pronounced as previously reported.
vibrational symmetry is not the determining factor of reactivity, but rather the localization of the vibrational amplitude at the transition state.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
vibrational activation of dissociative chemisorbption is state-selective, but the state-selectivity is a function of the symmetry of the vibration.
vibrational symmetry is an important parameter in the activation of the dissociation of CH4 on metal surfaces.
the symmetry of the initial vibrational excitation is important in the reactivity of the CH4/Pt(111) reaction.
The main takeaway from our work is that
vibrational symmetry can be used to control reactivity.
vibrational activation of methane chemisorption on Pt(111) is not a purely vibrational effect but depends on the symmetry of the vibration.
symmetry considerations can be used to predict the reactivity of a given vibration.
